writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Merge Intervals when it asks for calendar consolidation and covered ranges. Here the concrete task is: Return merged closed intervals. The visible input `[(1,3),(2,6),(8,10),(9,12)]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. When the method sorts intervals or events, use the coordinate and tie break required by its proof. Other greedy walks keep an invariant without sorting. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Sort by start and extend the current interval while the next one overlaps. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A greedy step commits to a local choice. Give the exchange or dominance reason that an optimal solution can still include that choice. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n log n) time · O(n) output; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `1-6,8-12` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test touching intervals, equal endpoints, empty input, and a locally attractive choice that blocks a better future choice. Keep interval endpoint conventions explicit where they apply. If sorting is part of the method, its Rust comparator must encode the proof's exact tie break. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
